summary:
Mission Control: Orbital is an interactive 3D browser game, built with React, TypeScript and Three.js, that takes players through a complete Earth-observation space mission. Players start with a mission briefing that sets their objectives, a $120M budget and a 650 kg mass limit. They then build a satellite in a 3D Assembly Lab from 23 real-world parts, including solar wings, batteries, reaction wheels, flight computers, antennas, imagers and radar. Every part changes mass, cost and power, and players can start from a template or a free sandbox.

Next they choose an orbit (LEO, Sun-synchronous or MEO) and an Earth target such as rainforests or Arctic ice, then watch a launch sequence. In live operations, the satellite circles a 3D Earth. Players manage battery power through eclipses, aim instruments at their target, and send data down to the real Goldstone, Svalbard and Canberra ground stations while random space events disrupt the mission.

A final mission report scores objectives, power management, engineering and science out of 1,000. It awards badges and explains what went well and what to improve next time. The game turns real mission trade-offs into hands-on learning.
details:
Mission Control: Orbital is an interactive 3D simulation that runs in your browser and follows a satellite through its whole life. There are three core stages:

  1. Build: Users put together an observation satellite part by part, including the power system, solar panels, antenna, sensors and thrusters. Each part shows what it does, what it costs, and what happens if you leave it out.
  2. Launch: Users choose an orbit and send the satellite into space.
  3. Mission control: With the satellite in orbit, users watch it circle Earth and work out when it can reach ground radio stations. Altitude and antenna design decide how often contact happens and how long it lasts. When a connection opens, the satellite sends its data back to Earth.

Core benefits:

  • It takes something abstract and expensive (spacecraft engineering) and makes it hands-on and easy to grasp. Users learn by actually doing something, leaving a part out or picking the wrong orbit has visible consequences, and that sticks better than reading . It builds strategic thinking, because users have to balance cost against performance and find the best mix of parts for their mission. It’s free and runs in a browser, with nothing to download or install.

Our objective:
We want young people to get curious about space and see engineering as something they could do. By the end, users should understand how satellites orbit, what’s inside them, what they cost and how they talk to Earth. We also hope they come away making decisions more logically and weighing trade-offs, which helps well beyond space.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • [HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website and interface]
  • [Three.js (or Babylon.js / Unity WebGL) for the 3D satellite, Earth and orbit]
  • [Blender or free 3D models for the satellite parts]
  • [GitHub for version control and hosting]
  • [AI tools such as Claude, if you used them to help build it]
  • Reference material from NASA, including the Design and Develop Science Missions guide, CubeSat 101, NASA Mission Visualization and the Webb “Build It Yourself” game, so that parts, costs and orbits stay realistic.

How is the project creative?
Most satellite resources are either static diagrams or professional tools that beginners find too hard. Ours sits between the two. It’s a game with a story, from building to launching to running the mission, and the user’s choices shape the outcome. Linking the antenna and the altitude directly to when the satellite can reach radio stations shows a real engineering constraint in a way people can see and play with. In most educational tools, that part stays hidden.

The factors we considered:

  • Audience: It’s mainly for young people, so we kept the language simple, the visuals engaging and the controls easy.
  • Accuracy vs simplicity: Parts, costs and orbit behavior are based on real NASA material but simplified so beginners aren’t overwhelmed.
  • Accessibility: It runs in a browser, so anyone with a computer and internet can use it.
  • Engagement: Every choice has a consequence, which keeps users interested and teaches them through trade-offs.
  • Time and skills: We scoped the project to what our team could build well during the hackathon.
